## Research context

We are generating ideas in the area of: **Target: AAAI 2026
Track: Information Retrieval and Text Mining (or Machine Learning: Theory)

Direction: Establish formal expressiveness bounds for multi-vector (MaxSim/Chamfer) retrieval representations — the sign-rank equivalent for ColBERT-style late interaction. While LIMIT (ICLR 2026) proved that single-vector embeddings have fundamental capacity limitations tied to sign-rank, no formal theory exists for what multi-vector representations with sum-of-max scoring can express. We aim to characterize the representational capacity of MaxSim as a function of the number of vectors per document and their dimensionality, providing tight bounds analogous to sign-rank for inner products.

Seed Papers:
- Weller et al., "On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval" (ICLR, 2026) — Proves single-vector limitations via sign-rank; the direct theoretical anchor we extend
- Wang et al., "R^{2k} is Theoretically Large Enough for Embedding-based Top-k Retrieval" (arXiv, 2026) — Proves dimension sufficiency for single-vector; our work must be consistent with or subsume this
- Dhulipala et al., "MUVERA: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings" (NeurIPS, 2024) — Algorithmic reduction of MaxSim to inner product with approximation guarantees; does NOT address expressiveness
- Jacob et al., "On Strengths and Limitations of Single-Vector Embeddings" (arXiv, 2026) — Empirically confirms multi-vector superiority on LIMIT but uses only toy math models; explicitly lacks formal theory
- Khattab & Zaharia, "ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction" (SIGIR, 2020) — Introduced MaxSim; foundational architecture whose expressiveness we characterize

Known Gaps:
- No formal characterization of the representational capacity of sum-of-max-inner-product scoring as a function of number of vectors and dimensionality
- No proven separation result showing which relevance patterns multi-vector can represent that single-vector provably cannot (beyond empirical demonstrations on LIMIT)
- No connection between MaxSim expressiveness and communication complexity or combinatorial dimensions analogous to sign-rank

Theoretical Anchor: Sign-rank of binary matrices characterizes single-vector embedding capacity (Weller et al.). MaxSim scoring over k vectors per document can be viewed as a richer communication protocol where each party sends k messages instead of one. The analogous complexity measure — potentially related to partition number or multi-round communication complexity — should yield tighter and more favorable bounds, formally explaining multi-vector superiority.

Constraints:
- Compute: ≤200 H100-hours (primarily theoretical; compute needed only for empirical validation on LIMIT and synthetic constructions)

Quality Self-Checks:
- [x] Core insight: Multi-vector retrieval's empirical superiority over single-vector can be formally characterized through communication complexity, yielding provable separation results.
- [x] Why not obvious: Sign-rank gives clean bounds for inner products but sum-of-max-inner-products introduces combinatorial structure (assignment problems) that breaks standard techniques — requires novel proof strategies.
- [x] Baseline fear test: A simple 'multi-vector is at least as expressive as single-vector' result would be trivial; we need tight bounds showing HOW MUCH more expressive, as a function of the number of vectors.
- [x] Information exploited: The structure of MaxSim as a combinatorial optimization (max-matching) over inner products — this algebraic structure is what enables stronger representational capacity and what existing analyses ignore.

Avoid:
- Purely empirical comparisons of single-vector vs multi-vector (already done extensively; adds nothing new)
- Loose existential bounds that only show multi-vector CAN be better without quantifying the gap
- Ignoring computational complexity — bounds that require exponentially many vectors per document are theoretically interesting but practically useless
- Conflating approximation guarantees (MUVERA-style) with expressiveness characterization — these are orthogonal questions**

# Summary of "Dual VC Dimension Obstructs Sample Compression by Embeddings"

## Abstract Overview

The paper investigates whether arbitrary VC classes can be embedded into well-structured VC classes while maintaining comparable dimensions. The authors prove an impossibility result: "for every $d$ there is a class with VC dimension $d$ that cannot be embedded in any extremal class of VC dimension smaller than exponential in $d$."

## Main Technical Results

**Primary Finding:** The research establishes that extremal classes with VC dimension $d$ have dual VC dimension bounded by $2d+1$. This contrasts sharply with the classical Assouad bound of $2^{d+1}-1$ for general concept classes.

**Stronger Result:** The authors prove that $2d+1$ also upper bounds the dual Radon number of extremal classes, extending classical convex geometry theorems to broader combinatorial settings using topological methods.

## Learning Theory Implications

The findings directly challenge the Floyd-Warmuth approach to the sample compression conjecture. That strategy proposes embedding arbitrary VC classes into extremal classes with comparable dimension, then applying optimal compression schemes. However, this work demonstrates such embedding requires exponential dimension increase in some cases, producing compression schemes potentially exponentially worse than the conjecture predicts.

**Key Contribution:** The research combines topological methods and Radon theorem variants to establish fundamental limits on embedding strategies.

# Analysis of "Dual VC Dimension Obstructs Sample Compression by Embeddings"

## Full Abstract Summary

The paper investigates whether arbitrary VC classes can be embedded into well-behaved extremal VC classes. The authors demonstrate this is fundamentally limited, proving that "for every $d$ there is a class with VC dimension $d$ that cannot be embedded in any extremal class of VC dimension smaller than exponential in $d$."

## Key Results

**Main Theorem on Dual VC Dimension:**
The authors establish that extremal classes with VC dimension $d$ have dual VC dimension bounded by $2d+1$. This represents a dramatic improvement over the classical Assouad bound of $2^{d+1}-1$ for general concept classes—an exponential reduction in the upper bound.

**Stronger Result:**
They prove the dual Radon number of extremal classes is also bounded by $2d+1$, extending classical Radon theorem concepts into wider combinatorial frameworks without relying on Euclidean convexity.

## Critical Implications for Sample Compression

The results obstruct the Floyd-Warmuth approach to the sample compression conjecture. This strategy proposed embedding VC classes into comparable-dimension extremal classes, then applying optimal compression schemes. However, the authors demonstrate this approach would sometimes yield compression schemes "at least exponentially larger than what is predicted by the sample compression conjecture."

## Technical Methods

The proof employs topological methods, specifically utilizing variants of the Topological Radon Theorem, enabling a structural abstraction applicable beyond classical convex geometry.

# MUVERA: Technical Overview of Fixed Dimensional Encodings

## Core Concept

MUVERA reduces multi-vector retrieval to single-vector MIPS by transforming sets of query and document embeddings into fixed-dimensional vectors whose dot product approximates Chamfer similarity. The system creates asymmetric mappings: distinct functions for queries and documents that enable retrieval through standard optimized MIPS algorithms.

## Technical Mechanism

### Random Partitioning Scheme

The foundation involves partitioning the embedding space ℝ^d into B clusters using a partition function φ. The technique leverages **"locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)"** to ensure nearby vectors land in identical clusters with higher probability. Specifically, the authors employ SimHash, which partitions space using k_sim random half-spaces, creating 2^(k_sim) clusters.

For each cluster k, the method constructs block vectors:
- Query block: sum of all query embeddings mapping to cluster k
- Document block: centroid of document embeddings in that cluster

### Inner Product Approximation

The blocked vectors are defined such that their dot product becomes:

⟨q⃗, p⃗⟩ = Σ(k=1 to B) Σ(q∈Q, φ(q)=k) [1/|P∩φ^(-1)(k)|] Σ(p∈P, φ(p)=k) ⟨q,p⟩

This formulation approximates the Chamfer sum by concentrating matching pairs within cluster boundaries. When multiple document embeddings occupy the same cluster, using their centroid minimizes distortion from collisions.

### Dimensionality Reduction

The initial dimension dB can be reduced through random projections ψ applied per block. Each block undergoes multiplication by a random ±1 matrix, scaling to dimension d_proj < d. Multiple independent repetitions (R_reps) enhance approximation quality, yielding final dimension d_FDE = B · d_proj · R_reps.

## Theoretical Guarantees

**Theorem 2.1** establishes that with appropriately configured parameters, FDEs provide ε-additive approximations to normalized Chamfer similarity. The normalized version divides Chamfer by |Q|, ensuring values remain in [-1,1]. The approximation holds in expectation and with probability 1-δ.

**Theorem 2.2** demonstrates that FDEs enable **"ε-approximate nearest neighbor"** recovery in improved runtime O(|Q|·max{d,n}·(1/ε^4)·log(m/ε)·log n), compared to brute-force Chamfer computation of O(|Q|·max_i|P_i|·n).

## Connection to Locality-Sensitive Hashing

SimHash exploits LSH properties to group similar vectors. By computing signs of dot products with random Gaussian vectors, it creates collision-dependent hash buckets. Normalized vectors naturally align with this approach, as implemented in ColBERT embeddings. The LSH guarantee ensures nearest neighbors have elevated collision probability, allowing cluster-based matching to recover high-quality Chamfer neighbors effectively.

The **"fill_empty_clusters"** mechanism strengthens this connection by assigning empty clusters to their nearest document embedding, preventing loss of potential matches while maintaining the LSH collision structure.

# Generative Retrieval as Multi-Vector Dense Retrieval: Key Insights

## Core Equivalence Proof

The paper establishes that generative retrieval (GR) and multi-vector dense retrieval (MVDR) share a unified framework for computing query-document relevance. The authors demonstrate this through rigorous mathematical derivation by analyzing the decoder architecture of GR models.

The pivotal finding shows that GR's training loss can be reformulated as:

**rel(d,q) = sum(Ẽ_d^T · Q ⊙ A)**

This mirrors MVDR's framework: **rel(d,q) = sum(D^T · Q ⊙ A)**, where both use element-wise products of token vectors and an alignment matrix.

## Mathematical Framework

### The Alignment Matrix (A)

The alignment matrix fundamentally controls which query-document token pairs contribute to relevance scoring. The authors identify this as central to both methods, explaining: "the alignment matrix...controls whether a document and query token pair can be matched and contribute to the relevance."

In MVDR (like ColBERT), the alignment employs sparse, heuristic matching—selecting the highest-scoring document token per query token. GR uses dense, learned alignment derived from attention mechanisms: **A = softmax(D̂^T · W^T · Q)**.

### Key Structural Properties

**Lemma 5.1** establishes that attention-based alignment matrices exhibit low-rank structure, bounded by ||A - R|| ≤ 4γ||W||, connecting both paradigms' theoretical foundations.

## Decoder Analysis

The critical insight emerges from examining GR's cross-attention layers. The authors trace how:

1. Cross-attention weights compute: **α_i = softmax(Q^T · W · d̂_{i-1})**
2. These weights create output: **h_i = W_V · Q · α_i**
3. Final logits combine embedding and attention: **e_{d_i}^T · h_i**

This decomposition reveals that GR implicitly performs multi-vector matching, not single-token lookup as previously assumed.

## Practical Implications

**Document Encoding Differences**: GR typically uses simple word embeddings (ẽ_d), while MVDR uses contextualized token vectors (D). Recent improvements like PAWA decoding and non-parametric (NP) decoding introduce contextualized representations into GR, aligning it more closely with MVDR's expressiveness.

**Alignment Direction Divergence**: MVDR performs "query-to-document alignment" (each query token finds its best document match), while GR implements "document-to-query alignment" (each predicted document token attends to relevant query tokens). Experiments confirm query-to-document alignment outperforms document-to-query in reranking scenarios.

**Term Matching Phenomenon**: Both methods exhibit strong exact-match preferences in their alignment patterns, despite using different matching mechanisms, suggesting semantic matching emerges organically from their architectures.

This theoretical bridge illuminates why GR and MVDR show comparable performance profiles and suggests pathways for hybrid approaches leveraging each method's strengths.

# Technical Details: Scaling Laws for Embedding Dimension in Information Retrieval

**Paper ID:** arXiv:2602.05062  
**Submitted:** February 4, 2026  
**Authors:** Julian Killingback, Mahta Rafiee, Madine Manas, Hamed Zamani

## Core Focus

The research investigates how retrieval performance scales with embedding dimension in dense retrieval systems, which encode queries and documents as dense vectors for similarity matching.

## Abstract Summary

The authors conduct "a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between embedding dimension and retrieval performance." They examine two model families across varying sizes to characterize scaling behavior comprehensively.

## Key Findings

**Power-Law Relationship:**
The research demonstrates that "the scaling behavior fits a power law," enabling derivation of scaling laws based solely on embedding dimension and joint laws incorporating both dimension and model size.

**In-Distribution Performance:**
For tasks aligned with training data, "performance continues to improve as embedding size increases, though with diminishing returns."

**Out-of-Distribution Performance:**
Notably, when "evaluation data that is less aligned with the training task" is used, results differ substantially. Performance becomes "less predictable, with performance degrading with larger embedding dimensions for certain tasks."

## Practical Implications

The authors position their work as offering "a practical guide for selecting model and embedding dimension to achieve optimal performance with reduced storage and compute costs."

## Document Details
- **Length:** 9 pages, 7 figures
- **Subjects:** Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
- **License:** CC BY 4.0

## Key Relationships

The log-rank conjecture asserts that for a Boolean matrix its communication complexity and the logarithm of its matrix rank over the reals are polynomially related.

An equivalent linear-algebraic formulation of the conjecture is that for Boolean matrices, the matrix rank and partitioning number (sometimes called the binary rank) are quasi-polynomially related.

## Sign-Rank and Partition Number

A recent formulation introduces a new parameter to understand these relationships: Signed rectangle rank is the minimum number of all-1 rectangles needed to express the Boolean matrix as a ±1-sum, and it lies between rank and partition number, with signed rectangle rank equivalent to rank up to a logarithmic factor.

## Constant Cost and Cancellations

The fundamental difference between these measures involves: Rank allows for cancellations in the summation, while partitioning is a monotone model where all-1 submatrices must be combined positively and disjointly.

These results show a hierarchical relationship: rank < signed rectangle rank < partition number, with recent work suggesting that the gap between signed rectangle rank and rank is much smaller than previously understood.
